opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the first big tests of the Responsible Scaling Policy actually being put into practice on a frontier training run, and I think a lot of what we learned was just operational.

The basic idea in the RSP is that you don't want to train a model all the way to the end, look at it, and then discover it crossed some capability threshold you were worried about. You want to be checking along the way. So during training we'd take intermediate checkpoints at regular intervals, measured in effective compute, and run them through a set of evaluations meant to tell us whether we were getting close to the next AI Safety Level. The things we cared most about were areas like biological and chemical misuse, cyber capabilities, and autonomous replication, the kinds of capabilities where crossing a line would mean we needed stronger safeguards before going further.

The coordination challenge is that these are very different teams with different timelines. On the pretraining side, you have a giant run going, and every day of compute is expensive, so you really don't want to pause unnecessarily. On the evaluation side, some of these evals are pretty involved. Some are automated and quick, but others involve red-teamers or domain experts actually interacting with the model, which takes time. So a lot of the work was building the pipeline so that as soon as a checkpoint was ready, it could flow to the right people, the evals could run fast, and results could come back while the run kept going.

We also built in a buffer. The policy wasn't "stop when you hit the threshold," it was more like: define warning signs that trigger well before the actual danger point, so there's room for the evaluations to lag a bit and you still have time to react. That buffer is what lets you keep training without constantly holding your breath.

Honestly, the first time through there were a lot of rough edges. Figuring out who makes the call, what counts as a concerning result versus noise, how to elicit capabilities well enough from a model that hasn't been fine-tuned yet so you're not underestimating it. That last one is really important, because a pretrained checkpoint can look less capable than it really is if you don't prompt it well. So a big lesson was that evaluations are a real research problem, not just a checklist, and you have to invest in them like one.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate checkpoints were evaluated for proximity to a safety threshold and that concerning results would require stronger safeguards before training continued, making the training plan depend on evaluation results.

r002.rationale: It explains that training time was expensive and describes a pipeline to run evaluations quickly and return results while training continued, avoiding unnecessary pauses.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it's harder than it sounds, and a lot of the difficulty is logistical rather than conceptual.

The way I'd frame it is: during a big pretraining run, the model is changing every day. You've got a checkpoint from this morning that's a bit better than the one from last week, and the question is always, "When do we actually stop and run the full battery of evaluations?" Because running the serious evals — the dangerous-capability evals in particular, the ones that feed into our Responsible Scaling Policy — is expensive. It's not just compute. It's people. You need the folks who built the eval to look at the results, interpret them, figure out whether a weird score is a real capability jump or just a formatting bug.

So for Claude 3, we basically had to commit in advance to a cadence. The RSP says you have to evaluate before you cross certain thresholds of effective compute, and the way we operationalised that was setting checkpoints — in the literal sense, saved model weights — where we'd say, "Okay, this one gets the full treatment." And that meant the pretraining team, which is my team, had to coordinate pretty closely with the evals and safety teams about what the schedule looked like. You can't just show up with a model and say, "Hey, is this one dangerous? We'd like to know by Friday."

The other thing that I think people underestimate is that the model you evaluate isn't quite the model you ship. The pretrained base model is different from the model after fine-tuning. And some capabilities only really show up once you've done the post-training work — once the model is actually willing to answer the question in a helpful way. So we had to think about: are we evaluating the base model, the fine-tuned model, or both? And the conservative answer is you want to look at the thing that's closest to what could actually cause harm, which usually means something post-trained, and often with some effort put into eliciting the capability rather than just asking once and taking the first answer.

And then there's the tension that I think about a lot, which is that there's real pressure to move fast. Not in a sinister way — it's just that a training run is going, people are excited, there's a product roadmap. And the evaluation step is sort of the thing that says, "Hold on." I actually think that's the point of having a written policy. It takes the decision out of the hands of whoever happens to be most enthusiastic in the moment and makes it a thing we've committed to in advance. For Claude 3 specifically, that mostly worked fine — the model came in below the thresholds we were worried about. But I'd say the process taught us a lot about where the friction is, and a bunch of what we changed afterwards was about making that coordination less painful so it's not something people are tempted to skip.

astra-6.text:
The way I thought about it was that evaluations had to be part of the training process, rather than something we did only once we’d decided the model was finished. You want to learn early enough that the results can actually change what you do.

There are a few different things to coordinate there: which capabilities you’re testing, when you’ll have a checkpoint that’s useful to test, and who needs the results to make a decision. And there’s a tension: you want to give the people doing evaluations plenty of time, but the model is still changing, so an earlier result might not tell you everything you need to know about the final version.

So the important thing is to have that feedback loop working throughout training, while preserving enough time to evaluate the model you’re actually considering releasing. And to be clear about what an evaluation establishes—because not finding a concerning capability isn’t necessarily the same as showing that it isn’t there.

sol-6.1.text:
There were really two coordination problems. One was figuring out what we needed to measure: which capabilities would matter for safety, and what evidence would tell us we were approaching a threshold in our responsible scaling policy? The other was making sure we could actually run those evaluations at useful points during training.

You don’t want to get to the end of a training run and only then discover that an evaluation needs weeks of preparation. So we tried to work backwards: get the relevant teams talking early, identify the evaluations that would take the longest, and arrange access to model checkpoints so that we could learn something before the final model was ready.

And there’s an important distinction between a model failing a test and us having good evidence that it lacks a capability. Maybe the prompting wasn’t very good, or the model needed tools, or the evaluation itself wasn’t measuring what we thought. So part of the coordination was making room to investigate results, rather than treating evaluation as a box you check at the end.
